# An Introduction to Hypothesis Testing

Hypothesis testing is an approach to *assessing a claim* about a population by analysing a sample of data. The claim will typically relate to some aspect of the distribution of a population of interest, often a *parameter* such as the *population mean*, $\mu$. The foundation of hypothesis testing lies in probability.

### The Logic of Hypothesis Testing {-}

\begin{itemize}[itemsep=0.5pt]
    \item A coin is tossed 50 times, and it lands showing tails 47 of those times.
    \item A six-sided die is rolled 80 times, and the average score across the 80 rolls is 5.4.
    \item A random number generator for integers from 1 to 10 returns a 7 twelve times in a row.
\end{itemize}



In each of these scenarios, there are two broad possible explanations:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ccc}
     & \textit{The coin and die are fair, and the number generator is working correctly,}& \\
     & \textit{but very unlikely results have occurred purely by chance...} & \\
     && \\
     & \textbf{or} & \\
     && \\
     & \textit{The coin is biased, the die rigged, the random number generator flawed...} &
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

A formal process is required to assess whether the observed result could reasonably be attributed to random chance, or whether there is sufficient evidence against this explanation. This process, called *hypothesis testing*, informs a substantial part of the remainder of the course.

\pagebreak

## The Null Hypothesis and the Alternative Hypothesis

A hypothesis test begins with two competing claims about a feature of one or more populations. Initially in this chapter, these claims will concern the population mean, $\mu$.

A conservative position is adopted as the starting point for the analysis. This claim is called the **null hypothesis**, denoted by $\text{H}_0$, and it is treated as the starting assumption unless the sample data provide sufficient evidence against it. The competing claim is called the **alternative hypothesis**, denoted by $\text{H}_1$.

These may be thought of *informally* as:

\begin{center}
    \begin{tabular}{lll}
        The null hypothesis & $\text{H}_0$ & \textit{``Nothing is happening.''}\\
        The alternative hypothesis & $\text{H}_1$ & \textit{``Something is happening.''}
    \end{tabular}
\end{center}

Both hypotheses should be formulated *before* examining the data to be analysed. It should also be decided whether evidence is being sought that the population mean is *less than* a specified value, *greater than* a specified value, or simply *different from* a specified value.

When the alternative hypothesis specifies a departure in only *one direction*, the test is described as **one-tailed**. When the alternative hypothesis allows for a departure in *either direction*, the test is described as **two-tailed**.




\begin{tcolorbox}[title=Example,colback=RoyalBlue!1!,colframe=RoyalBlue]
\textbf{Problem:} State the null and alternative hypotheses for each of the following claims.

\vspace{0.2cm}

\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(a)] The mean volume of liquid in espressos sold by a café is less than the 30ml stated on its menu. 
    \item[(b)] The mean mass of stoats in a woodland population is different from the previously measured 240g.
\end{enumerate}

\tcblower
\textbf{Solution:}
\begin{enumerate}
    \begin{multicols}{2}
    \item[(a)] $\text{H}_\text{0}:$  $\mu=\text{30}$\\ $\text{H}_\text{1}:$  $\mu<\text{30} \quad \textnormal{One-tailed test.}$
    \item[(b)] $\text{H}_\text{0}:$  $\mu=\text{240}$\\ $\text{H}_\text{1}:$  $\mu\ne\text{240} \quad \textnormal{Two-tailed test.}$
    \end{multicols}
\end{enumerate}
\end{tcolorbox}

## The Significance Level and the \textit{p}-value

The *true value* of a population parameter cannot be known by studying a sample. This means that, without a census of the entire population, a statistician will never say that they have *proved* or *disproved* a claim. A suitable conclusion should state whether the data provide *sufficient evidence to suggest* that the claim represented by the alternative hypothesis is valid, or *insufficient evidence* to do so. 

Once the null and alternative hypotheses have been stated, probability calculations are carried out using a starting assumption that *the null hypothesis is true*. The $\mathbf{\textit{p}}$\textbf{-value} is the probability, assuming the null hypothesis is true, of obtaining a result at least as extreme as the one observed, in the direction or directions specified by the alternative hypothesis.

The **significance level**, $\alpha$ (*"alpha"*), provides a threshold for deciding whether an observed result is sufficiently unlikely under the null hypothesis to justify rejecting it. The significance level should be decided before examining the data. A significance level of 5\% ($\alpha=\text{0.05}$) is commonly used when no other level has been specified.

When the $p$-value is less than or equal to $\alpha$, the result is described as *statistically significant*. Smaller $p$-values indicate stronger evidence against the null hypothesis.

\begin{centering}
\tcbset{width=16cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[adjusted title=The decision rule for the $p$-value and the significance level $\alpha$:, halign title = center,colback=red!5,colframe=red!70!black, halign = center,center]
\centering
If $p\text{-value}\leqslant\alpha$ then \textbf{reject }$\mathbf{\text{H}_\text{0}}$ and conclude that there is\newline \textit{sufficient evidence to suggest} that the claim represented by $\text{H}_\text{1}$ is valid.\\
\vspace{0.2cm}
If $p\text{-value}>\alpha$ then \textbf{do not reject }$\mathbf{\text{H}_\text{0}}$ and conclude that there is\newline \textit{insufficient evidence to suggest} that the claim represented by $\text{H}_\text{1}$ is valid.
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{centering}

Not rejecting the null hypothesis does not imply that it is true; it simply indicates that there is insufficient evidence against it. For this reason, the phrase 'accept $\text{H}_\text{0}$' should **not** be used.

\begin{tcolorbox}[title=Example,colback=RoyalBlue!1!,colframe=RoyalBlue]
\textbf{Problem:} A random sample of physics textbooks is weighed to assess whether the mean mass exceeds 570g. The hypotheses, chosen significance level and the $p$-value calculated for the data are shown below.

\vspace{-0.2cm}

\begin{center}
    \begin{tabular}{lll}
        $\text{H}_\text{0}:$  $\mu=\text{570}$ & \qquad\qquad & 10\% significance level \\
        $\text{H}_\text{1}:$  $\mu>\text{570}$ && $p\text{-value}=\text{0.0461}$
    \end{tabular}
\end{center}

\vspace{-0.2cm}

Write down a suitable conclusion to the hypothesis test.

\tcblower

Since $\text{0.0461}<\text{0.1}$, reject $\text{H}_\text{0}$ at the 10\% significance level.\newline There is sufficient evidence to suggest the population mean mass of a physics textbook exceeds 570g.

\end{tcolorbox}

## One-Sample \textit{z}-Test for the Population Mean using a \textit{p}-value

The *one-sample *$z$*-test for the population mean* is a hypothesis test used when a sample of data is taken from a population so that a claim about the value of the *population mean*, $\mu$, can be assessed. Since $z$-tests rely on assumptions about population parameters and the normal distribution, they are classed as **parametric tests**.

\begin{centering}
\tcbset{width=16cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[adjusted title=Conditions for the one-sample $z$-test for the population mean:, halign title = center,colback=red!5,colframe=red!70!black, halign = center]
\begin{itemize}
    \item The \textit{sampling distribution of the sample mean} is \textbf{normal}.
    \item The \textit{population standard deviation}, $\sigma$, is \textbf{known}.
    \item The observations are \textit{independent}, usually justified through \textbf{random sampling}.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{centering}

If a condition cannot be established from the information provided, it may be necessary to state an **assumption** under which the test would be valid. Any assumptions made should be identified, and their plausibility should be considered. For example, when a previously established value of $\sigma$ is used, it may be necessary to assume that the population standard deviation has remained \textit{unchanged}. 
 
When the sample size is greater than 20, the Central Limit Theorem can generally be invoked, allowing the sampling distribution of the sample mean to be treated as *approximately normal*. For the purposes of this course, when the sample size is sufficiently large, the sample standard deviation, $s$, may be used as an estimate of the population standard deviation, $\sigma$, allowing an approximate $z$-test to be performed.

Note in the example below that, with a sample mean of 257 observed, and an alternative hypothesis that the true population mean is *less than* 260, the $p$-value is the probability of observing a sample mean *as extreme or more extreme* than 257. In the context of a claim that $\mu<\text{260}$, the $p$-value is therefore $\text{P}\left(\bar{X}<\text{257}\right)$.

\begin{tcolorbox}[title=Example,colback=RoyalBlue!1!,colframe=RoyalBlue]
\textbf{Problem:} The designers of an electric car state that the distance that can be covered on a full charge is normally distributed, with a mean of 260 miles and a standard deviation of 10 miles. A car magazine randomly selects 14 of the cars from showrooms to be tested, with a sample mean of 257 miles obtained.\\[0.1em]

Stating one assumption required, perform a hypothesis test to assess, at the 1\% level of significance, the claim by the car magazine that the mean distance is actually less than the designers' claim.

\tcblower
\textbf{Solution:}
$\mu=\text{260}$, $\bar{x}=\text{257}$, $n=\text{14}$, $\sigma=\text{10}$\\

\vspace{0.02cm}

Assume that the standard deviation of the distance covered on a full charge remains 10 miles.\\

\vspace{0.1cm}

\begin{math}
\begin{array}{ll}
      \text{H}_\text{0}: & \mu=\text{260}\\
      \text{H}_\text{1}: & \mu<\text{260}
    \end{array}
\end{math}

\vspace{0.5cm}

Under $\text{H}_\text{0}$:\hspace{6cm}
\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture, overlay]
\begin{axis}[
  no markers, 
  domain=-3:3, 
  samples=100,
  ymin=0,
  axis lines*=left, 
  every axis y label/.style={at=(current axis.above origin),anchor=south},
  every axis x label/.style={at=(current axis.right of origin),anchor=west},
  height=3cm, 
  width=7cm,
  xtick=\empty, 
  ytick=\empty,
  enlargelimits=false, 
  clip=false, 
  axis on top,
  grid = major,
  hide y axis,
  hide x axis
  ]
\addplot [draw=none, fill=Black!20, domain=-3:-1.12] {gauss(x, 0, 1)} 
\closedcycle;
 \addplot [semithick] {gauss(x, 0, 1)};
\pgfmathsetmacro\valueA{gauss(-1.12,0,1)}
\pgfmathsetmacro\valueB{gauss(0,0,1)}
\fill[Black!20] (axis cs: -3,-0.02) rectangle (axis cs: -1.12,0);
\draw [semithick, black]  (axis cs:-1.12,-0.02) -- (axis cs:-1.12,\valueA);
\node[below] at (axis cs:-1.12,0)  {$-\text{1.12}$};
\node[above] at (axis cs: 0,\valueB)  {$Z$};
\node[below] at (axis cs: 0,0)  {0};
\node at (axis cs: -2.3,0.2)  {13.14\%};
\draw[semithick] (axis cs: -3,-0.02) -- (axis cs: 3,-0.02);
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}\\ 

\vspace{0.1cm}

$P(\bar{X}<\text{257})=P\left(Z<\dfrac{\text{257}-\text{260}}{\frac{\text{10}}{\sqrt{\text{14}}}}\right)=P(Z<-\text{1.12})=\text{0.1314}$\\

\vspace{0.1cm}

Since $\text{0.1314}>\text{0.01}$, do not reject $\text{H}_\text{0}$ at the 1\% level of significance. There is insufficient evidence to suggest that the mean distance the car can cover on a full charge is less than the stated 260 miles.

\end{tcolorbox}

\pagebreak

\begin{tcolorbox}[title=Example,colback=RoyalBlue!1!,colframe=RoyalBlue]
\textbf{Problem:} The mass of crisps dispensed into a sharing-sized bag by a machine is normally distributed with a mean of 150g and a standard deviation of 2g. After being serviced, a random sample of 30 bags gives a mean of 150.8g. Test at the 5\% significance level the claim that the machine now dispenses too much.

\tcblower
\textbf{Solution:}
$\mu=\text{150}$, $\bar{x}=\text{150.8}$, $n=\text{30}$, $\sigma=\text{2}$\\

\vspace{0.01cm}

\begin{math}
\begin{array}{ll}
      \text{H}_\text{0}: & \mu=\text{150}\\
      \text{H}_\text{1}: & \mu>\text{150}
    \end{array}
\end{math}

\vspace{0.3cm}

Under $\text{H}_\text{0}$:\hspace{7cm}
\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture, overlay]
\begin{axis}[
  no markers, 
  domain=-3:3, 
  samples=100,
  ymin=0,
  axis lines*=left, 
  every axis y label/.style={at=(current axis.above origin),anchor=south},
  every axis x label/.style={at=(current axis.right of origin),anchor=west},
  height=3cm, 
  width=7cm,
  xtick=\empty, 
  ytick=\empty,
  enlargelimits=false, 
  clip=false, 
  axis on top,
  grid = major,
  hide y axis,
  hide x axis
  ]
\addplot [draw=none, fill=Black!20, domain=2.19:3] {gauss(x, 0, 1)} 
\closedcycle;
 \addplot [semithick] {gauss(x, 0, 1)};
\pgfmathsetmacro\valueA{gauss(2.19,0,1)}
\pgfmathsetmacro\valueB{gauss(0,0,1)}
\fill[Black!20] (axis cs: 3,-0.02) rectangle (axis cs: 2.19,0);
\draw [semithick, black]  (axis cs:2.19,-0.02) -- (axis cs:2.19,\valueA);
\node[below] at (axis cs:2.19,0)  {2.19};
\node[above] at (axis cs: 0,\valueB)  {$Z$};
\node[below] at (axis cs: 0,0)  {0};
\node at (axis cs: 3,0.2)  {1.43\%};
\draw[semithick] (axis cs: -3,-0.02) -- (axis cs: 3,-0.02);
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}\\ 

\vspace{-0.1cm}

$\text{P}(\bar{X}>\text{150.8})=\text{P}\left(Z>\dfrac{\text{150.8}-\text{150}}{\frac{\text{2}}{\sqrt{\text{30}}}}\right)=\text{P}(Z>\text{2.19})=\text{0.0143}$\\[0.2em]

Since $\text{0.0143}<\text{0.05}$, reject $\text{H}_\text{0}$ at the 5\% level of significance. There is sufficient evidence to suggest that the mean mass of crisps dispensed per bag is more than 150g.

\end{tcolorbox}

For a *two-tailed* test, the probability of such an extreme result *in either direction* must be considered.

For the example below, this equates to the probability of observing a sample mean with a difference of 1 gram or more from 82. Given a symmetrical distribution of the test statistic, such as with a $z$-test, a $p$-value for a two-tailed test is *double* the initial probability obtained by only considering the probability in *one* direction. 

\begin{tcolorbox}[title=Example,colback=RoyalBlue!1!,colframe=RoyalBlue]
\textbf{Problem:} A tomato grower has been monitoring the mass of the tomatoes they grow, with the mean mass of a tomato shown to be 82 grams. Following a change in the soil composition in which they are grown, the grower wants to see whether the mean mass of their tomatoes has been affected.\\[0.1em]

A sample of 36 tomatoes gives a mean mass of 83 grams and a standard deviation of 3 grams. It is assumed that the sample standard deviation is a reliable estimate of the population standard deviation.\\[0.1em]

Perform a hypothesis test to determine whether there is evidence to suggest that the mean mass of their tomatoes has changed, stating one further assumption required and justifying the validity of the test with reference to the sample size.

\tcblower
\textbf{Solution:}
$\mu=\text{82}$, $\bar{x}=\text{83}$, $n=\text{36}$, $\sigma\approx \text{3}$\\

\vspace{0.01cm}

Assume that the sample of tomatoes was random. Since $n=36>\text{20}$, the distribution of the sample mean is approximately normally distributed regardless of the underlying distribution of the mass of a tomato.\\

\vspace{0.2cm}
\begin{math}
\begin{array}{ll}
      \text{H}_\text{0}: & \mu=\text{82}\\
      \text{H}_\text{1}: & \mu\ne \text{82}
    \end{array}
\end{math}

\vspace{0.5cm}

Under $\text{H}_\text{0}$:\hspace{7cm}
\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture, overlay]
\begin{axis}[
  no markers, 
  domain=-3:3, 
  samples=100,
  ymin=0,
  axis lines*=left, 
  every axis y label/.style={at=(current axis.above origin),anchor=south},
  every axis x label/.style={at=(current axis.right of origin),anchor=west},
  height=3cm, 
  width=7cm,
  xtick=\empty, 
  ytick=\empty,
  enlargelimits=false, 
  clip=false, 
  axis on top,
  grid = major,
  hide y axis,
  hide x axis
  ]
\addplot [draw=none, fill=Black!20, domain=-3:-2] {gauss(x, 0, 1)} 
\closedcycle;
\addplot [draw=none, fill=Black!20, domain=2:3] {gauss(x, 0, 1)} 
\closedcycle;
 \addplot [semithick] {gauss(x, 0, 1)};
\pgfmathsetmacro\valueA{gauss(-2,0,1)}
\pgfmathsetmacro\valueC{gauss(2,0,1)}
\pgfmathsetmacro\valueB{gauss(0,0,1)}
\fill[Black!20] (axis cs: 3,-0.02) rectangle (axis cs: 2,0);
\fill[Black!20] (axis cs: -3,-0.02) rectangle (axis cs: -2,0);
\draw [semithick, black]  (axis cs:2,-0.02) -- (axis cs:2,\valueA);
\draw [semithick, black]  (axis cs:-2,-0.02) -- (axis cs:-2,\valueA);
\node[below] at (axis cs:2,0)  {2};
\node[below] at (axis cs:-2,0)  {$-\text{2}$};
\node[above] at (axis cs: 0,\valueB)  {$Z$};
\node[below] at (axis cs: 0,0)  {0};
\node at (axis cs: 3,0.2)  {2.28\%};
\node at (axis cs: -3,0.2)  {2.28\%};
\draw[semithick] (axis cs: -3,-0.02) -- (axis cs: 3,-0.02);
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}\\

\vspace{-0.05cm}

$\text{P}(\bar{X}>\text{83})=\text{P}\left(Z>\dfrac{\text{83}-\text{82}}{\frac{\text{3}}{\sqrt{\text{36}}}}\right)=\text{P}(Z>\text{2})=\text{0.0228}$\\

\vspace{0.1cm}

$p$-value $=\text{2} \times \text{0.0228} = \text{0.0456}$ and $\alpha=\text{0.05}$\\[0.1em]

Since $\text{0.0456}<\text{0.05}$, reject $\text{H}_\text{0}$ at the 5\% level of significance. There is sufficient evidence to suggest that the mean mass of the grower's tomatoes has changed from 82 grams.

\end{tcolorbox}

#### [Exercise 10.3](#ex103a) {-}

\begin{enumerate}
    \item A practice question is below, followed by a student's \textbf{flawed} solution, featuring a number of issues.
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colback=white,colframe=black!50]
\textbf{Practice question:} The mass of dried tea leaves contained in each bag sold by tea company \textit{Brewed Awakenings} is known to be normally distributed with a standard deviation of 0.4 grams, and the mean amount contained in each bag should be 2.5 grams. It is suspected that the company's new machine is putting too little dried tea into each bag. The contents of a random sample of 10 bags are measured, and the mean mass obtained from this sample is 2.3 grams.\\[0.5em] Assume that the population standard deviation in mass of dried tea leaves per bag remains unchanged. Perform a $z$-test to assess whether the population mean mass of dried tea dispensed into each bag by the new machine is less than 2.5 grams, at the 5\% level of significance.

\tcblower
\textbf{Student's flawed solution:}\\

\begin{math}
\begin{array}{ll}
      \text{H}_\text{0}: & \text{mean}=\text{2.5}\\
      \text{H}_\text{1}: & \text{mean}< \text{2.5}
    \end{array}
\end{math}\\

Under $\text{H}_\text{0}$:\hspace{7cm}

## One-Sample \textit{z}-Test for the Population Mean using a Test Statistic

Obtaining a $p$-value in the previous section required calculating the probability of the observed sample mean, $\bar{x}$, by first using the $z$*-transformation for a sample mean* to obtain what is called a $z$*-score*. Instead of concluding a $z$-test by comparing a $p$-value to the significance level, an alternative approach is to compare the $z$-score, referred to as the **test statistic**, to predetermined cut-off values, called **critical values**.

\begin{centering}
\tcbset{width=10cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[adjusted title=For a one-sample $z$-test for the population mean:, halign title = center,colback=red!5,colframe=red!70!black, halign = center]
Test statistic: $z=\dfrac{\bar{x}-\mu}{\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}}$
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{centering}

A $z$*-test statistic* of 0 occurs when the sample mean of the observed data is equal to the value for $\mu$ claimed by the null hypothesis. The further the test statistic is from 0, the more extreme the observed data are.

*Critical values* can be found by first considering *critical regions*. These are the most extreme regions of the sampling distribution of the test statistic; if the calculated test statistic lies within these regions, the null hypothesis is rejected. Critical values are the *boundaries* of these critical regions. Below are examples of critical regions (shaded), and critical values (shown below the axis), for a $z$ test statistic with a 5\% level of significance.

For a one-tailed test, the most extreme 5\% of the distribution in the tail of interest is considered.

For a two-tailed test, the 5\% least likely observed values for the test statistic *in either direction* are considered. The significance level is split between 2.5\% in the upper tail and 2.5\% in the lower tail. The symmetry of the distribution means that the values to the left of the mean are the *negative* of the equivalent values on the right.

If the test statistic lies \textbf{within the critical region} then $\mathbf{\text{H}_\text{0}}$ is \textbf{rejected}, and so there is \textit{sufficient} evidence to suggest that the  alternative hypothesis is valid. If the test statistic lies \textbf{outwith the critical region} then $\mathbf{\text{H}_\text{0}}$ is \textbf{not rejected}, and so there is \textit{insufficient} evidence to suggest that the alternative hypothesis is valid.

Note that the following examples approach problems already covered in the examples for the previous section, which used a *p*-value approach, and lead to identical conclusions to the hypothesis tests conducted.

\begin{tcolorbox}[title=Example,colback=RoyalBlue!1!,colframe=RoyalBlue]
\textbf{Problem:} The designers of an electric car state that the distance that can be covered on a full charge is normally distributed, with a mean of 260 miles and a standard deviation of 10 miles. A car magazine randomly selects 14 of the cars from showrooms to be tested, with a sample mean of 257 miles obtained.\\[0.1em]

Stating one assumption required, perform a hypothesis test to assess, at the 1\% level of significance, the claim by the car magazine that the mean distance is actually less than the designers' claim.

\tcblower
\textbf{Solution:}
$\mu=\text{260}$, $\bar{x}=\text{257}$, $n=\text{14}$, $\sigma=\text{10}$\\

\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{math}
\begin{array}{ll}
      \text{H}_\text{0}: & \mu=\text{260}\\
      \text{H}_\text{1}: & \mu<\text{260}
    \end{array}
\end{math}

\vspace{0.5cm}

Test statistic: $z=\dfrac{\text{257}-\text{260}}{\dfrac{\text{10}}{\sqrt{\text{14}}}}=-\text{1.12}$
\hspace{4cm}
\begin{tikzpicture}[overlay]
\begin{axis}[
  no markers,

  every axis x label/.style={at=(current axis.right of origin),anchor=west},

\pgfmathsetmacro\valueB{gauss(0,0,1)}
\pgfmathsetmacro\valueC{gauss(2.33,0,1)}
\draw [semithick, black]  (axis cs:-2.33,0) -- (axis cs:-2.33,\valueA);
\node[below] at (axis cs: 0,0)  {0}; 
\node[below] at (axis cs: -2.33, 0) {$-\text{2.33}$};
\draw[very thick] (axis cs: -1.12,0) -- (axis cs: -1.12,0.44) node[above] {$-\text{1.12}$};
\node[above] at (axis cs: -2.5,\valueA) {1\%};
\node[above] at (axis cs: 0,\valueB)  {$z$};

\vspace{0.2cm}

Critical value: $z=-\text{2.33}$\\

Since $-\text{1.12}>-\text{2.33}$, do not reject $\text{H}_\text{0}$ at the 1\% level of significance. There is insufficient evidence to suggest that the mean distance the car can cover on a full charge is less than the stated 260 miles.

\end{tcolorbox}

When choosing a critical value for a two-tailed test, in which there are two critical regions, the critical value with the same sign (positive or negative) as the observed test statistic should be used in the conclusion.

\begin{tcolorbox}[title=Example,colback=RoyalBlue!1!,colframe=RoyalBlue]
\textbf{Problem:} A tomato grower has been monitoring the mass of the tomatoes they grows, with the mean mass of a tomato shown to be 82 grams. Following a change in the soil composition in which they are grown, the grower wants to see whether the mean mass of their tomatoes has been affected.\\[0.1em]

A sample of 36 tomatoes gives a mean mass of 83 grams and a standard deviation of 3 grams. It is assumed that the sample standard deviation is a reliable estimate of the population standard deviation.\\[0.1em]

Perform a hypothesis test to determine whether there is evidence to suggest that the mean mass of their tomatoes has changed, stating one further assumption required and justifying the validity of the test with reference to the sample size.

\tcblower
\textbf{Solution:}
$\mu=\text{82}$, $\bar{x}=\text{83}$, $n=\text{36}$, $\sigma\approx \text{3}$\\

\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{math}
\begin{array}{ll}
      \text{H}_\text{0}: & \mu=\text{82}\\
      \text{H}_\text{1}: & \mu\ne \text{82}
    \end{array}
\end{math}

\vspace{0.5cm}

Test statistic: $z=\dfrac{\text{83}-\text{82}}{\dfrac{\text{3}}{\sqrt{\text{36}}}}=\text{2}$
\hspace{4cm}

#### [Exercise 10.4](#ex104a) {-}

\begin{enumerate}
    \item A packing process packages ground coffee into bags. The mass of each bag is normally distributed, with standard deviation 15g. To comply with the technical standards stipulated for the process, the mean mass of coffee per bag should be 500g. After a recent adjustment of some of the machinery involved in the process, a random sample of 25 bags is taken and the sample mean is found to be 512g.\\[0.5em] Assuming that the standard deviation is unchanged, test the claim that there has been a change in the mean mass of coffee per bag at the 5\% level of significance.
    \item The lengths of metal bars produced by a particular machine in a factory are normally distributed with mean length 420cm and standard deviation 12cm. The machine is serviced, after which a random sample of 80 bars gives a mean length of 423cm.\\[0.5em] Perform a parametric test to assess whether there is evidence at the 1\% level of significance of an increase in the mean length of the bars produced, assuming the standard deviation of bar length remains the same.
    \item In 1980 the mass of a herring in the North Sea was found to be normally distributed with a mean of 160g and a standard deviation of 10g. In 2020 a random sample of 15 herrings yielded a mean mass of 158g.\\[0.5em] Assuming that the standard deviation is unchanged, test at the 1\% level of significance the hypothesis that the mean mass has decreased since 1980.
    \item The mass of a pack of salt is normally distributed with a mean of 200g and a standard deviation of 12g. After servicing, it is suspected that the salt dispensing machine is not dispensing the same mean amount of salt. A sample of 23 bags yields a mean mass of 205g per pack.\\[0.5em] Stating two assumptions required, test the hypothesis that the mean amount of salt dispensed by the machine is no longer 200g.
    \item Last season, the mean distance a player ran per game by the players of a football team was 7.1km. This season, a random selection of players are observed for a randomly chosen game each, and the distances they run are recorded.
    \begin{center}
    \begin{tabular}{|p{5.4cm}|p{3cm}|}
        \hline
            Sample size & 26\\
        \hline
            Sample mean & 7.3km\\
        \hline
            Sample standard deviation & 0.7km\\
        \hline
    \end{tabular}
    \end{center}
    It is assumed that the sample size is sufficiently large that the sample standard deviation is a reliable estimate of the population standard deviation.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Perform a $z$-test to assess the evidence, at the 5\% level of significance, that the mean distance players are covering in a game this season has changed.
        \item Explain why the sample size may help support the use of a $z$-test for this data.
    \end{enumerate}
    \item A popular type of loaf sold by a regional chain of bakeries has been previously observed to have a mean mass of 500g, with a standard deviation of 20g. Following a change in the recipe used for the loaves, a random sample of 25 loaves yielded a mean mass of 483g. 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item State the condition for a sample size which implies that a sample mean will be approximately normally distributed even whilst the underlying distribution is not normally distributed.
        \item State one assumption required for the valid use of a $z$-test for the population mean loaf mass.
        \item Test at the 5\% significance level the claim that the mean mass of a loaf has decreased.
    \end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}

    \texttt{n = 23}\qquad \texttt{sample mean = 10.9}\qquad \texttt{sample SD = 2.3}\\
    \texttt{alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 12}\\

Assume that the sample standard deviation of spend per teacher is a reliable estimate of the population standard deviation.
    \begin{enumerate}

## One-Sample \textit{t}-Test for the Population Mean

In the early 20th century William Sealy Gosset, statistician and Head Experimental Brewer at the Guinness factory in Dublin, developed a method for analysing a sample mean when the population standard deviation is unknown and must be estimated using the sample standard deviation. This was necessary since he was working with **small sample sizes**, for which the sample standard deviation could not be used as a reliable estimator for the population standard deviation. Guinness restricted employees from publishing their work under their own names, so Gosset published under the pseudonym *Student*. The distribution that he described became known as **Student's** **_t_** **-distribution**, or simply *the* $t$-*distribution*.

Not knowing the population standard deviation, $\sigma$, introduces additional uncertainty about the distribution of the sample mean, with the **sample standard deviation**, $s$, used instead. This results in a $t$-distribution that resembles a normal distribution but with *fatter tails*. The $t$-distribution takes one parameter called **degrees of freedom**, denoted using the Greek letter $\nu$. For the one-sample $t$-test for population mean, the degrees of freedom can be calculated for a sample size $n$ as $\nu=n-\text{1}$.

The one-sample $t$-test for population mean is a **parametric test** that should be used in place of the equivalent $z$-test when the population standard deviation, $\sigma$, is unknown, and the sample standard deviation, $s$, is to be used instead. Whilst in this course $z$-tests are often asked for when sample sizes are large, when the underlying distribution is normal, the $t$-test remains the *exact* test when the $\sigma$ is unknown $s$ is used instead.

\begin{centering}
\tcbset{width=16cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[adjusted title=Conditions for the one-sample t-test for the population mean:, halign title = center,colback=red!5,colframe=red!70!black, halign = center]
\begin{itemize}
    \item The \textit{underlying population} is \textbf{normally distributed}.
    \item The observations are \textit{independent}, usually justified through \textbf{random sampling}.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{centering}

The $t$-test statistic is identical to that of the equivalent $z$-test, except the use of the sample standard deviation, $s$, instead of the population standard deviation, $\sigma$.

\begin{centering}
\tcbset{width=12cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[adjusted title=For a one-sample t-test for the population mean:, halign title = center,colback=red!5,colframe=red!70!black, halign = center]
Test statistic: $t=\dfrac{\bar{x}-\mu}{\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}}$ \; with $\nu=n-\text{1}$ degrees of freedom
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{centering}

Whilst $t$-tests will typically be conducted using a *test statistic* approach, computer output for $t$-tests may instead return $p$-values. For all hypothesis tests, $p$-values can be interpreted through comparison against the chosen significance level, $\alpha$.

Critical values for the $t$-test can be found on *page 13* of the Data Booklet, referring to the significance level, whether the test is one-tailed or two-tailed and the degrees of freedom; constructing a sketch of the distribution is often useful. As the sample size increases, and hence $\nu$ increases, the $t$-distribution approaches the normal distribution. This is why the Data Booklet provides a set of critical values for use when $\nu>\text{40}$, which match critical values for $z$-tests.

\pagebreak

\begin{tcolorbox}[title=Example,colback=RoyalBlue!1!,colframe=RoyalBlue]
\textbf{Problem:} A supermarket sells sharing-sized bags of a particular brand of crisps. A consumer watchdog is asked to investigate a claim that the mean mass of crisps contained in a bag is less than the stated contents of 150 grams. A random sample of bags gives the following results, in grams:

\vspace{-0.2cm}

  \begin{center}
  \begin{tabular}{c c c c c c c c} 
      148 & 151 & 149 & 152 & 145 & 150 & 146 & 151\\ 
  \end{tabular}
  \end{center}

\vspace{-0.2cm}

Stating a required assumption, perform a parametric test to assess the claim at the $\alpha=\text{0.01}$ level.

\tcblower
\textbf{Solution:}
$\mu=\text{150}$, $\bar{x}=\text{149}$, $n=\text{8}$, $s=\text{2.51}$\quad (calculating $\bar{x}$ and $s$ from the sample)\\

Assume that the mass of crisps in a bag is normally distributed.\\

\begin{math}
\begin{array}{ll}
      \text{H}_\text{0}: & \mu=\text{150}\\
      \text{H}_\text{1}: & \mu<\text{150}
    \end{array}
\end{math}

\vspace{0.5cm}

Test statistic: $t=\dfrac{\text{149}-\text{150}}{\dfrac{\text{2.51}}{\sqrt{\text{8}}}}=-\text{1.127}$
\hspace{3cm}
\begin{tikzpicture}[
    overlay,
    declare function={
        student(\x)=0.384991*(1+(\x*\x)/7)^(-4);
    }
]
\begin{axis}[
    no markers,
    domain=-4:4,
    samples=150,
    ymin=0,
    axis lines*=left,
    height=3cm,
    width=6.5cm,
    xtick=\empty,
    ytick=\empty,
    enlargelimits=false,
    clip=false,
    axis on top,
    hide y axis,
    hide x axis
]

% Shaded rectangular strip below the curve
\fill[black!50]
    (axis cs:-4,-0.04)
    rectangle
    (axis cs:-2.998,0);

% Shaded critical region below the t-density
\addplot[
    draw=none,
    fill=black!50,
    domain=-4:-2.998
] {student(x)}
\closedcycle;

% t_7 density
\addplot[semithick] {student(x)};

% Horizontal axis
\draw
    (axis cs:-4,-0.04) --
    (axis cs:4,-0.04);

% Critical-value boundary
\draw[semithick,black]
    (axis cs:-2.998,-0.04) --
    (axis cs:-2.998,0.0159);

% Axis and distribution labels
\node[below] at (axis cs:0,-0.04) {0};
\node[above] at (axis cs:0,0.384991) {$t_7$};

% Critical value and tail probability
\node[below] at (axis cs:-2.998,-0.04) {$-\text{2.998}$};
\node[above] at (axis cs:-3.3,0.0159) {1\%};

% Test statistic
\draw[very thick]
    (axis cs:-1.127,-0.04) --
    (axis cs:-1.127,0.47)
    node[above] {$-\text{1.127}$};

\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}\\

Degrees of freedom: $\nu=n-\text{1}=\text{8}-\text{1}=\text{7}$\\

Critical value: $t=-\text{2.998}$\\

Since $-\text{1.127}>-\text{2.998}$, do not reject $\text{H}_\text{0}$ at the 1\% level of significance. There is insufficient evidence to suggest that the mean mass of crisps in a bag is less than the stated value of 150g.

\end{tcolorbox}

Assumptions and other comments should be written carefully and with reference to context. For example:

\begin{tabular}{p{4cm}l}
\textit{Missing context:} & "Assume the data is normally distributed."\\
\textit{With context:} & "Assume that the \textbf{mass of crisps in a bag} is normally distributed."
\end{tabular}

\begin{tcolorbox}[title=Example,colback=RoyalBlue!1!,colframe=RoyalBlue]
\textbf{Problem:} Marks scored in an exam are known to be approximately normally distributed, and historically the mean mark achieved by students is 72. After some minor tweaks to the exam, marks gained by a random sample of 7 students generated the summary data below. Perform a hypothesis test at the 5\% level of significance to determine whether there is evidence that the difficulty of the exam has changed for students.\\

\vspace{-0.8cm}

\begin{center}
$\Sigma x=\text{571} \qquad \qquad \Sigma x^\text{2}=\text{46851} \qquad \qquad n=\text{7}$
\end{center}

\tcblower
\textbf{Solution:}
$\mu=\text{72}$, $\bar{x}=\text{81.57}$, $n=\text{7}$, $s=\text{6.754}$\\

\begin{math}
\begin{array}{ll}
      \text{H}_\text{0}: & \mu=\text{72}\\
      \text{H}_\text{1}: & \mu\ne \text{72}
    \end{array}
\end{math}

\vspace{0.5cm}

Test statistic: $t=\dfrac{\text{81.57}-\text{72}}{\dfrac{\text{6.754}}{\sqrt{\text{7}}}}=\text{3.749}$
\hspace{3cm}

    declare function={

    }
]

    },

] {student(x)}
\closedcycle;

\addplot[
    draw=none,

] {student(x)}

% t_6 density
\addplot[semithick] {student(x)};

% Horizontal axis

    (axis cs:-4,-0.04) --

% Critical-value boundaries

% Critical values

    {$-\text{2.447}$};

% Tail probabilities
\node[above] at (axis cs:-2.9,0.0339)

Degrees of freedom: $\nu=n-\text{1}=\text{7}-\text{1}=\text{6}$\\

Critical value: $t=\text{2.447}$\\

Since $\text{3.749}>\text{2.447}$, reject $\text{H}_\text{0}$ at the 5\% level of significance. There is sufficient evidence to suggest that the mean mark achieved by students is no longer 72, and that the difficulty of the exam has changed.

\end{tcolorbox}

#### [Exercise 10.5](#ex105a) {-}

\begin{enumerate}
    \item The amount of sugar contained in frozen pizzas, per 100g, is normally distributed. A random sample of 8 brands of frozen pizza gives the following sugar content per 100g, measuring in grams:
    \begin{center}
    \begin{tabular}{c c c c c c c c} 
      3.5 & 2.1 & 5.3 & 4.4 & 3.4 & 2.2 & 4.1 & 5.0\\ 
    \end{tabular}
    \end{center}
    Test at the 5\% significance level the claim that the mean sugar content per 100g in a frozen pizza is less than 5 grams.
    \item In a game of football, the amount of time between a goal being scored and the game resuming is normally distributed. The time taken to resume, in seconds, is recorded for a random sample of 6 goals, with results:
    \begin{center}
    \begin{tabular}{c c c c c c} 
      49 & 25 & 31 & 23 & 38 & 29\\ 
    \end{tabular}
    \end{center}
    Test at the 10\% level of significance the claim that the mean time taken for a game to resume after a goal is greater than the 30 seconds that is generally considered to be typical.
    \item A camera tripod can supposedly safely hold masses of up to 4.5kg. A photography shop disputes this figure, and randomly selects 10 tripods. Each is loaded progressively with heavier masses until it fails. The results, in kg are summarised as follows:
    \begin{center}
    \begin{tabular}{c c c} 
      $n=\text{10}$ & $\Sigma x=\text{40.5}$ & $\Sigma x^\text{2}=\text{165.49}$\\ 
    \end{tabular}
    \end{center}
    Stating an assumption required, test at the 1\% level the claim that the mean mass the tripods can withstand before failure is actually less than 4.5kg.
    \item \textit{Vinho Verde} is a type of Portuguese wine that originated in the Minho Province in the far north of the country. In 2009, the University of Minho supported a study which examined the extent to which wine quality can be judged through measuring its physicochemical properties. As part of the study, the acidity level of a random sample of 11 white \textit{Vinho Verde} wines all made using the \textit{alvarinho} grape were measured. The summary data obtained from this sample was as follows (measured in $pH$):
    \begin{center}
    $\Sigma x=\text{34.89} \qquad \qquad \Sigma x^\text{2}=\text{110.81}$
    \end{center}
Worldwide, the mean acidity level of white wines is 3.4 $pH$.\\[1em]
Stating one assumption required, perform a parametric test at the 5\% level of significance to determine whether the white \textit{Vinho Verde} wines made from the \textit{alvarinho} grape differ in acidity level from white wines made worldwide.
    \item A \textit{soporific drug} is one which has been shown to induce sleep, and increase drowsiness. An early 20th century study into possibly soporific drugs involved giving ten patients a dose of one such drug and recording whether they reported sleeping \textit{more} than usual that night (recorded as a positive number) or \textit{less} than usual (recorded as a negative number). The results recorded, in hours, were:
    \begin{center}
    \begin{tabular}{cccccccccc} 
      0.7 & -1.6 & -0.2 & -1.2 & -0.1 & 3.4 & 3.7 & 0.8 & 0.0 & 2.0\\ 
    \end{tabular}
    \end{center}
    The study wished to determine whether there was evidence from the study of the drug leading to increased sleep. Perform a hypothesis test to assess the evidence at the 2.5\% level of significance.
\end{enumerate}

A random sample of 14 such bass guitars gives the following masses, in pounds:
    \begin{center}

      9.5 & 9.4 & 9.7 & 9.6 & 9.3 & 9.8 & 9.7
    \end{tabular}
    \end{center}
    Perform a hypothesis test at the 1\% level of significance to assess evidence for the claims.
\item An experiment was conducted to measure and compare the effectiveness of various feed supplements on the growth rate of chickens. As part of this, 14 newly hatched chicks were randomly selected to be given a soybean-based feed supplement. Their masses in grams after six weeks were recorded, and the following summary statistics were obtained:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ccccccc}
variable & n & min & max & mean & sd\\
  \hline
weight (grams) & 14 & 158.0 & 329.0 & 246.4 & 54.1\\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
It has historically been observed that the mean mass of a chick after six weeks is 260 grams. Stating one assumption required, perform a hypothesis test to determine whether there is evidence at the 5\% level of significance that giving a soybean-based supplement affects the mass a chick will reach by six weeks.
    \item The second-most common species of tree in the United States is the \textit{loblolly pine}, regarded as one of the most commercially important species of tree in the Southeastern US for its timber. A survey based on a sample of 15 of the loblolly trees in one region revealed a sample mean height of 32.4 feet and a variance of 4.285 $\text{feet}^2$. The heights of the trees are known to be normally distributed. Stating one assumption required, test at the 1\% significance level whether the data provide evidence to suggest the mean height of loblolly trees in the region is greater than 30 feet.
    \item A school is looking to figure out a new course for the annual school cross-country competition. The goal is that the new course will have a mean time of 45 minutes for the pupils to complete it. The first ten pupils to respond to a request by the PE department for volunteers to test the course have their time taken to complete the course recorded. The results of the $t$-test used to assess whether the course meets their requirements is as follows:\vspace{0.5cm}\\
    \texttt{t-test for the population mean}\\
    \texttt{n = 10}\qquad \texttt{sample mean = 53.1}\qquad \texttt{sample SD = 11.2492}\\
    \texttt{alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 45}\\
    \texttt{t = }\textbf{****}\qquad \texttt{p-value = 0.0488}\\
    \vspace{0.1cm}
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item State the null and alternative hypotheses for the test conducted.
        \item Determine the missing value of the $t$-test statistic, indicated by \textbf{****} in the computer output.
        \item Find the critical value for the hypothesis test, at the 5\% level of significance.
        \item Use the $p$-value to write a conclusion to the hypothesis test.
        \item Name the sampling method used and comment on the appropriateness. 
    \end{enumerate}
    \item An experiment into the cold tolerance of a species of grass plant looked at the effect of low temperature on its carbon dioxide (CO2) uptake. It is known that, under normal conditions, the CO2 uptake rate for the species is known to be 33 $\mu \text{mol}/\text{m}^\text{2}$, whilst the sample of 7 areas exposed to chilling resulted in a sample mean uptake of 29.97 $\mu \text{mol}/\text{m}^\text{2}$ and a standard deviation of 8.335 $\mu \text{mol}/\text{m}^\text{2}$. Perform a parametric test to assess the evidence for CO2 uptake being affected by low temperature for the grass plant, at the 10\% level of significance.
\end{enumerate}

\pagebreak

## One-Sample \textit{z}-Test for the Population Proportion

If $X$ elements from a random sample of size $n$ from a population of interest satisfy some condition, then the **sample proportion**, $\hat{P}$, can be calculated as:

$$\hat{P}=\frac{X}{n}$$

For example, if a survey of registered voters reveals 114 out of 250 intend to vote for the incumbent candidate, the *sample proportion*, $\hat{p}$, is $\frac{\text{114}}{\text{250}}=\text{0.456}$. The true value of the **population proportion**, **_p_**, may differ from this value. The **one-sample $z$-test for population proportion** assesses whether an *observed sample proportion* provides statistically significant evidence against a *null-hypothesised population proportion*. The test statistic can be derived from the distributions of the random variables $X$ and hence $\hat{P}$:

\vspace{-0.3cm}

$$X \sim \text{B}(n,p)$$ 

When $np>\text{5}$ and $nq>\text{5}$, $X$ is *approximately* normally distributed:

\vspace{-0.3cm}

\begin{align*}
\text{E}(X) & = np\\
\text{V}(X) & = npq\\
X & \approx \mathsf{N}(np,npq)
\end{align*}

The distribution of $\hat{P}$ can now be obtained since $\hat{P}=\dfrac{X}{n}$:

$$\mathsf{E}\left(\hat{P}\right)=\text{E}\left(\frac{X}{n}\right)=\frac{\text{1}}{n}\text{E}(X)=\frac{\text{1}}{n}\times np=p$$

$$\text{V}\left(\hat{P}\right)=\text{V}\left(\frac{X}{n}\right)=\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)^\text{2} \text{V}(X)=\frac{\text{1}}{n^\text{2}}\times npq=\frac{pq}{n}$$
Therefore:

\vspace{-0.2cm}

$$\hat{P} \approx N\left(p,\frac{pq}{n}\right)$$

The $z$-transformation leads to the required test statistic:

\begin{centering}
\tcbset{width=10cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[adjusted title=For a one-sample $z$-test for the population proportion:, halign title = center,colback=red!5,colframe=red!70!black, halign = center]
Test statistic: $z=\dfrac{\hat{p}-p}{\sqrt{\dfrac{pq}{n}}}$
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{centering}

Note that $\sqrt{\dfrac{pq}{n}}$ is called the **standard error of the sample proportion**.

\begin{centering}
\tcbset{width=15cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[adjusted title=Conditions for the one-sample z-test for the population proportion:, halign title = center,colback=red!5,colframe=red!70!black, halign = center]
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\mathbf{\textbf{\emph{np}}>\text{5}}$ \textbf{ and } $\mathbf{\textbf{\emph{nq}}>\text{5}}$
    \item The observations are \textit{independent}, usually justified through \textbf{random sampling}.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{centering}

\pagebreak

Critical values for the $z$-test for population proportion are determined in the same way as for the $z$-test for the population mean.

\begin{tcolorbox}[title=Example,colback=RoyalBlue!1!,colframe=RoyalBlue]
\textbf{Problem:} A data storage company knows that 10\% of the hard drives they use will fail within a year of being installed. They have decided to trial the use of a cheaper model of hard drive, but are concerned that it may have a higher failure rate. During this trial, 60 of the new hard drives are randomly selected to be monitored for a year once installed. Of those 60, 11 fail within a year.\\ 

Use a parametric hypothesis test to assess the evidence, at the 5\% level of significance, that the new drives have a higher first-year failure rate than the previous model.

\tcblower
\textbf{Solution:}
$p=\text{0.1}$ , $q=\text{0.9}$ , $n=\text{60}$ , $\hat{p}=\frac{\text{11}}{\text{60}}=\text{0.183}$\\

\vspace{0.2cm}

\begin{math}
\begin{array}{ll}
      \text{H}_\text{0}: & p=\text{0.1}\\
      \text{H}_\text{1}: & p>\text{0.1}
    \end{array}
\end{math}\\

\vspace{0.2cm}

Test statistic: $z=\dfrac{\text{0.183}-\text{0.1}}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\text{0.1} \times \text{0.9}}{\text{60}}}}=\text{2.14}$
\hspace{3cm}
\begin{tikzpicture}[overlay]
\begin{axis}[
  no markers, 
  domain=-3:3, 
  samples=100,
  ymin=0,
  axis lines*=left, 
  every axis y label/.style={at=(current axis.above origin),anchor=south},
  every axis x label/.style={at=(current axis.right of origin),anchor=west},
  height=3cm, 
  width=6.5cm,
  xtick=\empty, 
  ytick=\empty,
  enlargelimits=false, 
  clip=false, 
  axis on top,
  grid = major,
  hide y axis
  ]
\addplot [draw=none, fill=black!50, domain=1.64:3] {gauss(x, 0, 1)} \closedcycle;
 \addplot [semithick] {gauss(x, 0, 1)};
\pgfmathsetmacro\valueA{gauss(1.64,0,1)}
\pgfmathsetmacro\valueB{gauss(0,0,1)}
\draw [semithick, black]  (axis cs:1.64,0) -- (axis cs:1.64,\valueA);
\node[below] at (axis cs: 0,0)  {0};
\node[above] at (axis cs: 0,\valueB)  {$z$};
\node[below] at (axis cs: 1.64, 0) {1.64};
\node[above] at (axis cs: 1.8,\valueA) {5\%};
\draw[very thick] (axis cs: 2.14,0) -- (axis cs: 2.14,0.44) node[above] {2.14};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}\\


Critical value: $z=\text{1.64}$\\


Since $\text{2.14}>\text{1.64}$, reject $\text{H}_\text{0}$ at the 5\% level of significance. There is sufficient evidence to suggest that the proportion of the new hard drives that fail within their first year of use is higher than 10\%.

\end{tcolorbox}

Since the alternative hypothesis for this test refers to the population *proportion*, conclusions should always aim to refer to a 'proportion' in context (and never the *mean*).

\begin{tcolorbox}[title=Example,colback=RoyalBlue!1!,colframe=RoyalBlue]
\textbf{Problem:} A candidate in a mayoral election claims that 85\% of voters intend to vote for them. Out of a random sample of 80 people eligible to vote, 59 say that they intend to vote for that candidate. Perform a hypothesis test to assess the evidence at the 1\% level of significance that their claim may be untrue, justifying the use of a $z$ test for this data.

\tcblower
\textbf{Solution:}
$p=\text{0.85}$ , $q=\text{0.15}$ , $n=\text{80}$ , $\hat{p}=\frac{\text{59}}{\text{80}}=\text{0.7375}$\\

$np=\text{80}\times \text{0.85}=\text{68}$ and $nq=\text{80}\times \text{0.15}=\text{12}$.

Since $np>\text{5}$ and $nq>\text{5}$, a normal approximation is appropriate.\\

\vspace{0.2cm}

\begin{math}
\begin{array}{ll}
      \text{H}_\text{0}: & p=\text{0.85}\\
      \text{H}_\text{1}: & p\ne \text{0.85}
    \end{array}
\end{math}\\

\vspace{0.2cm}

Test statistic: $z=\dfrac{\text{0.7375}-\text{0.85}}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\text{0.85} \times \text{0.15}}{\text{80}}}}=-\text{2.82}$
\hspace{3cm}
\begin{tikzpicture}[overlay]
\begin{axis}[
  no markers, 
  domain=-3:3, 
  samples=100,
  ymin=0,
  axis lines*=left, 
  every axis y label/.style={at=(current axis.above origin),anchor=south},
  every axis x label/.style={at=(current axis.right of origin),anchor=west},
  height=3cm, 
  width=6.5cm,
  xtick=\empty, 
  ytick=\empty,
  enlargelimits=false, 
  clip=false, 
  axis on top,
  grid = major,
  hide y axis
  ]
\addplot [draw=none, fill=black!50, domain=2.58:3] {gauss(x, 0, 1)} \closedcycle;
\addplot [draw=none, fill=black!50, domain=-3:-2.58] {gauss(x, 0, 1)} \closedcycle;
 \addplot [semithick] {gauss(x, 0, 1)};
\pgfmathsetmacro\valueA{gauss(2.58,0,1)}
\pgfmathsetmacro\valueB{gauss(0,0,1)}
\draw [semithick, black]  (axis cs:2.58,0) -- (axis cs:2.58,\valueA);
\draw [semithick, black]  (axis cs:-2.58,0) -- (axis cs:-2.58,\valueA);
\node[below] at (axis cs: 0,0)  {0};
\node[above] at (axis cs: 0,\valueB)  {$z$};
\node[below] at (axis cs: 2.58, 0) {2.58};
\node[above] at (axis cs: 3.2,\valueA) {0.5\%};
\node[below] at (axis cs: -2.58, 0) {$-\text{2.58}$};
\node[above] at (axis cs: -3.2,\valueA) {0.5\%};
\draw[very thick] (axis cs: -2.82,0) -- (axis cs: -2.82,0.44) node[above] {$-\text{2.82}$};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}\\


Critical value: $z=-\text{2.58}$\\


Since $-\text{2.82}<-\text{2.58}$, reject $\text{H}_\text{0}$ at the 1\% level of significance. There is sufficient evidence to suggest that the true proportion of voters intending to vote for that candidate is not 85\%, and that the candidate's claim may be untrue.

\end{tcolorbox}

#### [Exercise 10.6](#ex106a) {-}

*For each question, show clearly that the conditions for the use of a normal approximation are satisfied.*

\begin{enumerate}
    \item A coin, which a student suspects may be biased, is thrown 500 times and 267 heads are obtained.\\[0.1em] Perform a $z$-test to assess whether the data provides sufficient evidence to suggest that the coin is biased, using a 10\% significance level.
    \item A newspaper claims that over 60\% of its readers are car owners. In a random sample of 312 readers there are 208 car owners. Suitable hypotheses are proposed of:
    \begin{center}
        \begin{math}
          \begin{array}{ll}
            \text{H}_\text{0}: & p=\text{0.6}\\
            \text{H}_\text{1}: & p>\text{0.6}
          \end{array}
      \end{math}
    \end{center}
    Test whether there is evidence at the 1\% level of significance to support the newspaper's claim.
    \item In a public opinion poll, 1000 randomly chosen teenagers were asked whether they would support a ban on mobile phones in schools.
    \begin{center}
    \begin{tabular}{|p{3.5cm}|p{3.5cm}|p{3.5cm}|}
    \hline
    Response & Yes & No\\
    \hline
    Frequency & 597 & 403\\
    \hline
    \end{tabular}
    \end{center}
    Test at the 5\% significance level whether the data supports an article's claim that 'a majority of teenagers support a ban on mobile phones in schools'.
    \item The proportion of left-handed people in the population is 10\%. A random sample of 400 surgeons found that 29 were left-handed. Perform a hypothesis test at the 5\% level of significance to assess whether there is evidence to suggest that the proportion of left-handed surgeons does not match the 10\% seen in the wider population.
    \item A seed company sells seeds in mixed packets and states that over 20\% of the resulting plants will have red flowers. A packet of seeds is sown by a gardener who finds that only 9 out of 82 plants have red flowers.\\[0.5em] Perform a hypothesis test to assess the claim that fewer than 20\% of the plants will actually have red flowers, using a 1\% significance level.
    \item In a factory, ready-sliced potatoes are cooked to make crisps, which are then placed into bags before flavouring is added and the bags sealed. Occasionally a packet of crisps is sealed without flavouring having been added. The crisp manufacturers have decided that they are content with this process provided no more than 1.8\% of bags are flavourless.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item A random sample of 50 bags is taken. Explain why performing a $z$-test for the proportion of flavourless crisps obtained from this sample would not be appropriate.
        \item Determine the minimum sample size required such that a $z$-test would be appropriate.
        \item From a much larger sample of 500 bags of crisps, 14 are found to be flavourless. Test at the 5\% level of significance whether the manufacturers should be concerned with the process.
    \end{enumerate}
    \item Scotland's 2022 census revealed that of those in employment, 7\% were working in construction. Last year, a random sample of 200 adults living in Scotland revealed that, of the 189 who were in some form of employment, only 8 were working in construction. Perform a parametric test to assess whether the data gives evidence at the 10\% level of significance that the proportion of working adults employed in construction has changed since the census.
    \pagebreak
    \item A football manager claims that the \textit{Video Assistant Referee} (VAR) system used in all games played in the top league leads to the on-field referee being instructed to watch a replay on a pitchside monitor in at least three-quarters of games. A journalist looks back every game played up to that point in the season.
    \begin{center}
    \begin{tabular}{|l|l|}
    \hline
    VAR instructed the referee to watch a replay & 38\\
    \hline
    VAR did not instruct the referee to watch a replay & 22\\
    \hline
    \end{tabular}
    \end{center}
    Assess at the 1\% significance level whether the data provides evidence to support the journalist's claim that the football manager was incorrect in their statement.
    \item A teacher says that the majority of pupils in a school prefer cats to dogs. A sample of pupils is asked which they prefer, with the results shown in the table below.
    \begin{center}
    \begin{tabular}{|p{3.5cm}|p{3.5cm}|}
    \hline
    Prefer cats & 17\\
    \hline
    Prefer dogs & 8\\
    \hline
    Total & 25\\
    \hline
    \end{tabular}
    \end{center}
    Perform a parametric test at the 5\% level of significance to assess whether the data provides evidence to support the teacher's claim, stating an assumption required.
    \item A popular chain of fast food restaurants states on its website that a vegan alternative to its most popular menu item is available in over 80\% of its restaurants. A researcher for a website that publishes articles on veganism and vegetarianism selects 60 of the chain's restaurants at random and asks one reader who lives near each restaurant to visit and see whether the vegan alternative is available.
    \begin{center}
    \begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|}
    \hline
    Vegan alternative available & Vegan alternative not available & Total \\
    \hline
    42 & 18 & 60\\
    \hline
    \end{tabular}
    \end{center}
    Perform a hypothesis test at the 5\% level of significance to assess whether the data suggests the chain is exaggerating the availability of the vegan alternative.

\item A manufacturer of rechargeable batteries claims that at least 95\% of its batteries remain operational after one year of normal use. A consumer organisation tests a random sample of 300 batteries and finds that 277 are still operational after one year.\\[0.1em]

Perform a hypothesis test at the 5\% level of significance to assess whether there is evidence that the manufacturer's claim is too optimistic.

\item In a recent election for a student representative, a candidate claimed before the vote took place that they would receive support from more than 55\% of students. After the election, a random sample of 500 ballot papers is checked and 256 are found to have been cast for the candidate.\\[0.1em]

Using a 10\% significance level, perform a hypothesis test to assess whether there is evidence that the candidate's claim was justified.

\item A wildlife charity states that 30\% of gardens in a particular area contain a bird feeder. A researcher randomly selects 150 gardens and observes that 58 contain a bird feeder.\\[0.1em]

Perform a hypothesis test at the 1\% significance level to determine whether the data provides evidence that the proportion of gardens containing a bird feeder differs from the value stated by the charity.
\end{enumerate}

## [Review Exercise](#re10a) {-}

\begin{enumerate}
    \item A pharmaceutical company has developed a drug designed to reduce the recovery time needed for a specific type of operation from the well-established mean time of 11 days. Following trials involving treating 24 randomly selected patients admitted to hospital for the operation with the drug, it is found that the mean recovery time for these patients is 9.6 days, with a standard deviation of 2.7 days.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Explain why a $z$-test can be used for this data despite the population standard deviation, $\sigma$, not being known.
        \item Perform a hypothesis test at the 1\% level of significance to assess the evidence that the drug may reduce the mean recovery time for the operation.
    \end{enumerate}
    \item A car company wishes to check that a new machine at their factory producing front bumpers is still maintaining the mean mass of 2.8kg for the part that the old machine produced. Eight bumpers produced by the new machine are randomly selected and weighed. The results, in kilograms, are:
    \begin{center}
    \begin{tabular}{c c c c c c c c} 
      2.9 & 2.6 & 3.3 & 3.1 & 3.0 & 2.9 & 3.1 & 2.8\\ 
    \end{tabular}
    \end{center}
    Perform a parametric test at the 5\% level of significance to determine whether there is sufficient evidence to suggest that the mean mass of the part produced by the new machine has changed from 2.8kg, stating an assumption required.
    \item The speed of cars passing through a village is being studied in an effort to improve safety for pedestrians, and is known to be normally distributed. The mean speed has previously been monitored over a number of years and found to be consistently at 33 mph, with a variance of 16 $\text{mph}^2$. Following the installation of speed bumps, the speed of 15 randomly selected cars is measured at the same point as before, with a sample mean of 31 mph observed. 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Perform a parametric test to determine whether the data provides evidence to support the council's claim that the speed bumps have been successful in reducing the mean speed of cars passing through the village.
        \item State an assumption required for the test conducted in part (a).
    \end{enumerate}
    \item A driving instructor posts an advert online stating nine out of ten of their students pass their driving test first time. A random sample of 60 students taught by the instructor reveals that only 47 of them passed their driving test first time. Perform a hypothesis test at the 1\% level of significance to assess the evidence for the claim that the proportion of students who pass first time is less than the instructor advertised.
    \item A coach working with a junior athletics club has observed for many years that the mean reaction time at the start of 100m races for the sprinters at the club has been consistently stable at 185 milliseconds. Claiming that this figure may no longer be valid, she randomly selects 8 sprinters and records their reaction time in their next races. None of the selected sprinters raced together in their next race. The summary data, where times were measured in milliseconds, is below:
    \begin{center}
    \begin{tabular}{c c c} 
      $n=\text{8}$ & $\Sigma x=\text{1372}$ & $\Sigma x^\text{2}=\text{237466}$\\ 
    \end{tabular}
    \end{center}
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Stating an assumption required, perform a $t$-test to test the coach's claim at the 10\% level of significance.
        \item The coach initially debated recording the reaction times of the eight sprinters competing in the gold medal race of club's annual 100m championships. Suggest one reason why she was correct to reject this approach.
    \end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}
